# Data Cleaning and Exploratory Data Analysis
This dataset has been filtered to only include auctions from 2006 and later. The dataset includes information on auction prices, dates, and other relevant features. We also have a separate dataset containing transaction information, which we will join with the auction data for further analysis.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
auctions <- read.csv("df_for_ml_improved_up_to_2012.csv")
transactions <- read.csv("transactions.csv") #charlie path
#transactions <- read.csv("/Users/tiernancolby/Downloads/transactions.csv") # Tiernan path

auctions <- auctions |>
    left_join(transactions, by = "case_id") |>
    filter(year >=2006)

write_csv(auctions, "joined_auctions_transactions.csv")
```


The complete dataset, composed of two joined tables, contains `r format(nrow(auctions), big.mark = ",")` observations and `r ncol(auctions)` variables before cleaning.

```{r}
#| label: clean-auctions
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)

MAX_SIDE_IN <- 300  # a side longer than this (inches) is treated as a unit error

raw <- read_csv("joined_auctions_transactions.csv",
                locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"),  # file is not UTF-8
                name_repair = "minimal",               # keep names like Tier...1
                guess_max = 30000, show_col_types = FALSE,
                col_types = cols(Year.of.Birth = col_character()))

# --- Helpers -----------------------------------------------------------------

unescape_html <- function(x) {
  str_replace_all(x, c("&#0?39;" = "'", "&#0?34;" = "\"", "&quot;" = "\"",
                       "&lt;" = "<", "&gt;" = ">", "&amp;" = "&")) |>
    str_squish()
}

# Collapse a block of 0/1 dummy columns into one factor ("unknown" if none is set)
from_dummies <- function(cols, labels = cols) {
  m <- as.matrix(raw[cols])
  m[is.na(m)] <- 0
  stopifnot(all(rowSums(m) <= 1))
  factor(if_else(rowSums(m) == 0, "unknown", labels[max.col(m, ties.method = "first")]))
}

# Same, for blocks named by a prefix, e.g. "Country...France"
from_prefix <- function(prefix) {
  cols   <- names(raw)[startsWith(names(raw), prefix)]
  labels <- str_remove(cols, fixed(prefix)) |>
    str_replace_all(fixed("."), " ") |>
    recode(Dutch = "Netherlands", Swiss = "Switzerland", Italia = "Italy")
  from_dummies(cols, labels)
}

# Genre codes are undocumented; labels inferred from known artists
genre_labels <- c("Painting", "Photograph", "Drawing", "Print", "Sculpture", "Other")
untitled_rx  <- regex("untitled|sans titre|senza titolo|ohne titel", ignore_case = TRUE)
multi_rx     <- regex("[\\[(]\\s*\\w+ works[\\])]", ignore_case = TRUE)

# --- Clean -------------------------------------------------------------------

auctions_clean <- raw |>
  mutate(
    across(c(artist_name, auction_house, nationality), unescape_html),

    # one-hot blocks -> single factors
    house_tier            = from_prefix("Tier..."),
    sale_country          = from_prefix("Country..."),
    sale_continent        = from_prefix("Continent..."),
    artist_country        = from_prefix("Living..."),
    artist_gender         = from_dummies(c("gender_female", "gender_male", "gender_NA"),
                                         c("female", "male", "unknown")),
    artist_education      = from_dummies(c("edu_domestic", "edu_abroad", "edu_both", "edu_NA"),
                                         c("domestic", "abroad", "both", "unknown")),
    artist_degree         = from_dummies(c("no_degree", "undergrad", "grad", "degree_NA"),
                                         c("none", "undergraduate", "graduate", "unknown")),
    artist_elite_school   = from_dummies(c("elite_school", "non_elite_school", "elite_school_NA"),
                                         c("elite", "non_elite", "unknown")),
    artist_elite_award    = from_dummies(c("elite_award_received", "elite_award_not_received"),
                                         c("received", "not_received")),

    # sale
    sale_date  = ymd(eventdate),
    sale_month = month(sale_date),
    is_hammer  = as.integer(Ham_Prem == "Hammer"),

    # prices
    log_price        = log(price_usd.x),
    log_price_real   = log(real_price_usd),
    log_estimate_mid = log(estimate_center_usd),

    # artwork: implausible sizes -> NA
    bad_size = replace_na(height.x > MAX_SIDE_IN | width.x > MAX_SIDE_IN, FALSE),
    across(c(height.x, width.x, size_inchsqr), \(v) replace(v, bad_size, NA)),
    log_area          = log(size_inchsqr),
    aspect_ratio      = height.x / width.x,
    work_age          = if_else(year - year_of_artwork >= 0, year - year_of_artwork, NA),
    genre             = factor(genre_labels[genre], levels = genre_labels),
    materials         = factor(materials),
    is_untitled       = as.integer(str_detect(replace_na(lot_title, ""), untitled_rx)),
    is_multiple_works = as.integer(str_detect(replace_na(lot_title, ""), multi_rx)),
    has_provenance    = as.integer(!is.na(provenance)),

    # artist: age -> NA if the birth record lists a death year or disagrees with age
    birth_year = as.integer(str_extract(Year.of.Birth, "\\d{4}")),
    bad_age    = str_detect(replace_na(Year.of.Birth, ""), fixed("d.")) |
                 replace_na(abs(year - birth_year - age) > 1, FALSE),
    artist_age     = replace(age, bad_age, NA),
    artist_has_bio = as.integer(biography == "Y")
  ) |>
  select(
    # ids
    row_id = case_id, is_train = train,
    # sale
    sale_date, sale_year = year, sale_month, auction_house, house_tier,
    sale_country, sale_continent, is_hammer,
    # prices (targets)
    price_usd = price_usd.x, price_real_usd = real_price_usd, log_price, log_price_real,
    # pre-sale estimates
    estimate_low_usd = estimate_min_usd, estimate_high_usd = estimate_max_usd, log_estimate_mid,
    # artwork
    genre, materials, height_in = height.x, width_in = width.x, area_sq_in = size_inchsqr,
    log_area, aspect_ratio, year_made = year_of_artwork, work_age,
    is_untitled, is_multiple_works, has_provenance,
    in_main_genre = matched_genre, sold_in_home_country = matched_country,
    # artist
    artist = artist_name, artist_nationality = nationality, artist_country, artist_age,
    artist_gender, artist_education, artist_degree, artist_elite_school,
    artist_elite_award, artist_has_bio,
    # artist reputation
    artist_rank = ranking, solo_shows = solo_show, group_shows = group_show,
    biennials = fest_biennal, private_collection_buys = private_inst,
    museum_buys = public_inst,
    # artist price history (earlier sales only)
    artist_sale_number = artwork_order,
    mean_price_last5_usd  = price_usd_prev_5_mean,  median_price_last5_usd  = price_usd_prev_5_median,
    mean_price_last10_usd = price_usd_prev_10_mean, median_price_last10_usd = price_usd_prev_10_median
  ) |>
  arrange(sale_date, row_id)
```

The final cleaned dataset contains `r format(nrow(auctions_clean), big.mark = ",")` observations and `r ncol(auctions_clean)` variables.

## Data dictionary: `auctions_clean`

Each row is one auction sale of a work by a living contemporary artist, 2006–2012. Binary columns are coded 0/1, and money is in USD.

**Leave out of the predictors:** all four price columns, because they are the outcome. The source's same-year price averages are dropped because they contain the sale's own price.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `row_id` | Unique row ID |
| `is_train` | Authors' time-based split: 1 = train (2006–2011), 0 = test (2011–2012) |
| `sale_date`, `sale_year`, `sale_month` | When the auction took place |
| `auction_house` | Auction house name |
| `house_tier` | House prestige tier, 1 (Christie's, Sotheby's, Phillips) to 4 |
| `sale_country`, `sale_continent` | Where the sale took place (smaller countries grouped as "Others") |
| `is_hammer` | 1 = the recorded price excludes the buyer's premium |
| `price_usd`, `log_price` | Sale price, nominal |
| `price_real_usd`, `log_price_real` | Sale price, adjusted for inflation |
| `estimate_low_usd`, `estimate_high_usd` | Auction house's pre-sale estimate range |
| `log_estimate_mid` | Log of the estimate midpoint. Known before the sale but very close to the price, so compare models with and without it |
| `genre` | Painting, Photograph, Drawing, Print, Sculpture or Other (labels inferred from undocumented codes) |
| `materials` | Materials code 1–17 (no key published) |
| `height_in`, `width_in`, `area_sq_in`, `log_area`, `aspect_ratio` | Size in inches. NA where a side was over 300 in (likely a unit error) |
| `year_made`, `work_age` | Year the work was made, and its age at sale |
| `is_untitled` | 1 = titled "Untitled" (or the French, Italian or German equivalent) |
| `is_multiple_works` | 1 = the lot is a set of works |
| `has_provenance` | 1 = the lot listed a provenance |
| `in_main_genre` | 1 = the work is in the artist's main genre |
| `sold_in_home_country` | 1 = sold in the country where the artist works |
| `artist` | Artist name. Use as a grouping variable or random effect |
| `artist_nationality`, `artist_country` | Nationality, and the country the artist lives in |
| `artist_age` | Age at sale. NA where the birth record was inconsistent |
| `artist_gender` | female / male / unknown |
| `artist_education` | Where they studied: domestic / abroad / both / unknown |
| `artist_degree` | none / undergraduate / graduate / unknown |
| `artist_elite_school`, `artist_elite_award` | Attended an elite art school; won an elite award |
| `artist_has_bio` | 1 = a biography was available |
| `artist_rank` | Global artist ranking at time of sale (lower = more prominent) |
| `solo_shows`, `group_shows`, `biennials` | Exhibition counts up to the sale year |
| `private_collection_buys`, `museum_buys` | Number of acquisitions by private collections and by museums |
| `artist_sale_number` | Position of this sale in the artist's auction history |
| `mean_price_last5_usd`, `median_price_last5_usd` | Mean and median price of the artist's previous 5 sales |
| `mean_price_last10_usd`, `median_price_last10_usd` | Same, for the previous 10 sales |



# Initial model fitting

```{r}
library(MASS)
```


```{r}
#plot(auctions_clean$log_price)
#plot(auctions_clean$price_usd)


# remove predictors 
model_df <- auctions_clean |>
  dplyr::select(
    -c(log_price, price_real_usd, log_price_real),                     # other transformations of the response
    -c(estimate_low_usd, estimate_high_usd, log_estimate_mid),         # experts' estimates of the response
    -c(row_id, sale_date, artist)                                      # ids / not predictors
  )
ols <- lm(price_usd ~ ., data = model_df)
summary(ols)

#transform y
bc <- boxcox(ols, lambda = seq(-0.3, 0.3, 0.01))
lambda <- bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
lambda_ci <- range(bc$x[bc$y > max(bc$y) - qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2])   # 95% CI for lambda
lambda
lambda_ci

# refit ols with transformed response
ols_y_trans <- lm(I(price_usd^(lambda)) ~ ., data = model_df)
summary(ols_y_trans)
```


From the Box-Cox transformation we use $\lambda =$ `r round(lambda, 3)`, the value that maximizes the profile log-likelihood. Its 95% confidence interval is [`r round(lambda_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(lambda_ci[2], 3)`], which does not contain $0$ (a log transformation) and does not contain $1$ (no transformation).  

The (almost) log transformation of the response raises the multiple $R^2$ of the OLS model from `r round(summary(ols)$r.squared, 3)` to `r round(summary(ols_y_trans)$r.squared, 3)`, an increase of `r round(summary(ols_y_trans)$r.squared - summary(ols)$r.squared, 3)`.

`r sum(is.na(coef(ols_y_trans)))` of the `r length(coef(ols_y_trans))` coefficients are estimated as NA. R does this when a column is an exact linear combination of others (for example, nested location categories), so the data contain perfect collinearity, on top of strong correlation among related predictors such as the size variables and the artist's previous sale prices.

Thus, we think that the model assumptions are not met. We check the model assumptions:

```{r}
plot(fitted(ols_y_trans), resid(ols_y_trans), xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0, col = "blue3")

qqnorm(resid(ols_y_trans))
qqline(resid(ols_y_trans), col = "blue3")

```


From the first plot it is hard to tell how much heterogenity we have, but certainly the variance of the first few residuals are a lot lower than the rest. From the second plots we see that the residuals are not normally distributed because they largely differ from the normal Q-Q plot.

Because of the collinearity and model assumptions, OLS is probably not a good approach here, so we will try other models such as lasso and ridge regression.

For the penalized models we model the log of the inflation-adjusted price, collapse factors with many rare levels, and drop rows with missing values. That removes `r format(nrow(auctions_clean) - nrow(model_df), big.mark = ",")` rows (`r round(100 * (nrow(auctions_clean) - nrow(model_df)) / nrow(auctions_clean), 1)`%), leaving `r format(nrow(model_df), big.mark = ",")` sales and `r ncol(x)` predictor columns. The data are split at random into `r format(length(y_train), big.mark = ",")` training and `r format(length(y_test), big.mark = ",")` test sales, and every model is scored on the same test set.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(glmnet)

# Predictors + response (log real price), with high-cardinality factors collapsed
model_df <- auctions_clean |>
  dplyr::select(
    -c(price_usd, log_price, price_real_usd),                  # other transformations of the response
    -c(estimate_low_usd, estimate_high_usd, log_estimate_mid), # experts' estimates of the response
    -c(row_id, sale_date, artist, is_train),                   # ids / not predictors
    -auction_house                                             # hundreds of levels; house_tier summarizes it
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(v) if_else(is.finite(v), v, NA))) |>  # Inf -> NA
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    artist_nationality = fct_lump_n(artist_nationality, 10),  # top 10 nationalities + "Other"
    artist_country     = fct_lump_n(artist_country, 10),      # top 10 countries + "Other"
    materials          = fct_lump_prop(materials, 0.01),      # codes with < 1% of rows -> "Other"
    genre              = fct_collapse(genre, Other = c("Other", "Sculpture"))  # Sculpture is ~1 row
  ) |>
  droplevels()

# Design matrix built once on all rows, so train and test share the same columns
x <- model.matrix(log_price_real ~ ., data = model_df)[, -1]
y <- model_df$log_price_real
stopifnot(nrow(x) == length(y))

nrow(auctions_clean) - nrow(model_df)   # rows dropped for missing values
ncol(x)                                 # number of predictor columns

# Random 75/25 train / test split (shared by every model below)
set.seed(1)
train_rows <- sample(nrow(x), size = floor(0.75 * nrow(x)))
x_train <- x[train_rows, ];  y_train <- y[train_rows]
x_test  <- x[-train_rows, ]; y_test  <- y[-train_rows]

# Test-set RMSE and R^2 (log scale), used for every model
test_metrics <- function(pred) {
  tibble(
    rmse = sqrt(mean((y_test - pred)^2)),
    r2   = 1 - sum((y_test - pred)^2) / sum((y_test - mean(y_test))^2)
  )
}
```

```{r}
# Lasso (alpha = 1), lambda chosen by 10-fold CV
set.seed(1)
lasso_fit <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1)
plot(lasso_fit)
c(lambda_min = lasso_fit$lambda.min, lambda_1se = lasso_fit$lambda.1se)

# Variables the lasso kept
coefs <- coef(lasso_fit, s = "lambda.1se")
lasso_coefs <- tibble(term = rownames(coefs), estimate = as.numeric(coefs)) |>
  filter(estimate != 0, term != "(Intercept)") |>
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))
nrow(lasso_coefs)   # number of predictors kept
lasso_coefs

lasso_pred <- as.numeric(predict(lasso_fit, newx = x_test, s = "lambda.1se"))
lasso_metrics <- test_metrics(lasso_pred)
lasso_metrics
```

Using $\lambda_{1se} =$ `r signif(lasso_fit$lambda.1se, 3)`, the lasso keeps `r nrow(lasso_coefs)` of the `r ncol(x)` predictor columns and sets the other `r ncol(x) - nrow(lasso_coefs)` to zero. The largest coefficients in absolute value belong to `r paste(head(lasso_coefs$term, 3), collapse = ", ")`. On the test set, the lasso has an RMSE of `r round(lasso_metrics$rmse, 3)` on the log scale (predictions are typically off by a factor of about `r round(exp(lasso_metrics$rmse), 2)`) and a test $R^2$ of `r round(lasso_metrics$r2, 3)`.



```{r}
# Ridge (alpha = 0), lambda chosen by 10-fold CV
set.seed(1)
ridge_fit <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0)
plot(ridge_fit)
c(lambda_min = ridge_fit$lambda.min, lambda_1se = ridge_fit$lambda.1se)

ridge_pred <- as.numeric(predict(ridge_fit, newx = x_test, s = "lambda.1se"))
ridge_metrics <- test_metrics(ridge_pred)
ridge_metrics
```

Ridge uses $\lambda_{1se} =$ `r signif(ridge_fit$lambda.1se, 3)`. It shrinks all `r ncol(x)` coefficients toward zero but keeps every predictor. Its test RMSE is `r round(ridge_metrics$rmse, 3)` and its test $R^2$ is `r round(ridge_metrics$r2, 3)`, slightly worse than" the lasso (`r round(lasso_metrics$r2, 3)`).  Interestingly enough, the lasso's smaller model slightly increases predictive accuracy. Ridge is often better when predictors are highly correlated, but here the lasso's variable selection seems to help. 

However, both lasso and ridge do not explain enough of the variance in the test set, so it makes sense to try a model that accounts for more complex, nonlinear relationships within the data.


```{r}
library(ranger)

# Same rows as the other models' train/test split; ranger handles factors directly
train_df <- model_df[train_rows, ]
test_df  <- model_df[-train_rows, ]
p <- ncol(train_df) - 1   # number of predictors

# Tuning grid
grid <- expand_grid(
  mtry          = c(floor(sqrt(p)), floor(p / 3), floor(p / 2)),
  min.node.size = c(5, 20)
)

# 5-fold CV on the training set
set.seed(1)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(train_df)))

cv_rmse <- function(mtry, min.node.size) {
  fold_mse <- map_dbl(1:5, \(k) {
    fit  <- ranger(log_price_real ~ ., data = train_df[folds != k, ],
                   num.trees = 300, mtry = mtry, min.node.size = min.node.size, seed = 1)
    pred <- predict(fit, train_df[folds == k, ])$predictions
    mean((train_df$log_price_real[folds == k] - pred)^2)
  })
  sqrt(mean(fold_mse))
}

cv_results <- grid |>
  mutate(cv_rmse = map2_dbl(mtry, min.node.size, cv_rmse)) |>
  arrange(cv_rmse)
cv_results
best <- slice(cv_results, 1)

# Final forest on the full training set with the best settings
rf_fit <- ranger(log_price_real ~ ., data = train_df,
                 num.trees = 500, mtry = best$mtry, min.node.size = best$min.node.size,
                 importance = "permutation", seed = 1)

rf_pred <- predict(rf_fit, test_df)$predictions
rf_metrics <- test_metrics(rf_pred)
rf_metrics

# Top 15 variables by permutation importance
tibble(variable = names(rf_fit$variable.importance),
       importance = rf_fit$variable.importance) |>
  slice_max(importance, n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(importance, fct_reorder(variable, importance))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Permutation importance (increase in MSE)", y = NULL)
```

Five-fold cross-validation picked `mtry` = `r best$mtry` (of `r p` predictors) and a minimum leaf size of `r best$min.node.size`, with a CV RMSE of `r round(best$cv_rmse, 3)`. On the test set the random forest has an RMSE of `r round(rf_metrics$rmse, 3)` and an $R^2$ of `r round(rf_metrics$r2, 3)`, compared with `r round(lasso_metrics$r2, 3)` for the lasso. The most important variable is `r names(which.max(rf_fit$variable.importance))`, and the top three are `r paste(names(sort(rf_fit$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE))[1:3], collapse = ", ")`.

## Model comparison and assumptions

```{r}
model_results <- bind_rows(
  lasso_metrics |> mutate(model = "Lasso", predictors = nrow(lasso_coefs)),
  ridge_metrics |> mutate(model = "Ridge", predictors = ncol(x)),
  rf_metrics    |> mutate(model = "Random forest", predictors = p)
) |>
  dplyr::select(model, predictors, rmse, r2) |>
  arrange(rmse)
model_results

# Test-set residuals for the linear (lasso) model
lasso_resid <- y_test - lasso_pred
plot(lasso_pred, lasso_resid, xlab = "Fitted (lasso)", ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0, col = "blue3")

qqnorm(lasso_resid)
qqline(lasso_resid, col = "blue3")
```

The best model on the test set is the `r tolower(model_results$model[1])`, with an RMSE of `r round(model_results$rmse[1], 3)` and an $R^2$ of `r round(model_results$r2[1], 3)`. The gap between the best and worst model is `r round(max(model_results$r2) - min(model_results$r2), 3)` in $R^2$.

**Assumptions.** Lasso and ridge are still linear models, so they assume the log price is linear in the predictors, and their residuals should look like the OLS residuals did. Penalization fixes the collinearity problem: it gives stable estimates where OLS returned NA. It does not fix non-normal or non-constant errors. Because we judge these models by cross-validation and test error, not by p-values, non-normal residuals matter less here than they did for OLS. The lasso's test residuals have a standard deviation of `r round(sd(lasso_resid), 3)`, and `r round(100 * mean(abs(lasso_resid) > 2 * sd(lasso_resid)), 1)`% of them are more than two standard deviations from zero (about 5% would be expected under normality). The random forest makes no linearity or normality assumption, so its higher test $R^2$ suggests that some of the relationships are nonlinear or involve interactions the linear models miss.

All of these models assume the sales are independent. They aren't fully independent, because the same artist appears many times and the random split puts the same artists in both the training and test sets. The test errors above are therefore likely somewhat optimistic for predicting prices of new artists.


# Obstacles and limitations

Because the dataset is large, both in number of observations and in number of predictors, we have to be careful about overfitting. The lasso and ridge help with this by penalizing large coefficients, but they still assume linearity. The random forest can capture nonlinear relationships, and protects against overfitting, but it is more difficult to interpret. With such a large dataset, it makes sense to prioritize predictive accuracy over interpretability. However, we will also try to understand the most important predictors and their effects on price. Modeling such a complex dataset using linear methods is a challenge, and it is difficult to confirm whether or not the assumptions of the models are met.
